claims.claim: Le Guin says a novel gains its power less from the sound of any single sentence than from the pacing and rhythm of paragraphs and chapters.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, "Reciprocity of Prose and Poetry" (1983), in Dancing at the Edge of the World (1989)
claims.quote: the pacing and rhythm of paragraphs and chapters

claims.claim: Le Guin praises a book she admires by calling its prose of unobtrusive excellence.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, blog 51, "The Narrative Gift as a Moral Conundrum", 2011
claims.quote: The prose is of unobtrusive excellence.

claims.claim: Le Guin says the sound and rhythm of prose is so different from poetry, being in a way much coarser.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin in conversation with David Naimon, excerpted from Ursula K. Le Guin: Conversations on Writing (Tin House, 2018), published at Literary Hub
claims.quote: the sound in the rhythm of prose, it is so different from poetry
claims.page: the poetry conversation, answer on Woolf and sound

claims.claim: Le Guin says the rhythms of a prose work are a very long beat.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin in conversation with David Naimon, Conversations on Writing (Tin House, 2018), excerpt at Literary Hub
claims.quote: long beat, the rhythms of a prose work
claims.page: the poetry conversation, answer on Woolf and sound

claims.claim: Le Guin says that, besides the long beat of the whole work, the sentence has its rhythms too.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin in conversation with David Naimon, Conversations on Writing (Tin House, 2018), excerpt at Literary Hub
claims.quote: Of course, the sentence has its rhythms too.
claims.page: the poetry conversation, answer on Woolf and sound

claims.claim: Le Guin says the deeper meaning that poetry shares with music is carried by the rhythm and the beat, the music of the sound.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin in conversation with David Naimon, Conversations on Writing (Tin House, 2018), excerpt at Literary Hub
claims.quote: it is the rhythm and the beat, the music of the sound that carries it
claims.page: the poetry conversation, answer on Macaulay and Swinburne

claims.claim: Le Guin says she does not think syllabically but rhythmically.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin in conversation with David Naimon, Conversations on Writing (Tin House, 2018), excerpt at Literary Hub
claims.quote: I don’t think syllabically, I think rhythmically.
claims.page: the poetry conversation, answer on haiku

claims.claim: Maslen argues that recording a diversity of understandings and ways of speaking inside a text written in a single language is the principal problem confronting Le Guin as a writer.
claims.source: Rob Maslen, "Towards an Archaeology of the Future: Theodora Kroeber and Ursula K Le Guin", Foundation: The Review of Science Fiction No. 67 (Summer 1996), text at The Anarchist Library
claims.quote: recording a diversity of different understandings and ways of speaking
claims.page: essay body, section on Semley's necklace

claims.claim: Le Guin describes Annals of the Parish as the annual records of a parish minister, kept and dated year by year for 50 years, from 1760 to 1810.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, "B-Sides: John Galt's Annals of the Parish", Public Books, 23 January 2017
claims.quote: kept and dated year by year for 50 years
claims.page: essay body, paragraph on the book's form

claims.claim: Le Guin calls the annalist narrator of that book a very old-fashioned narrator, and therefore reliable.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, "B-Sides: John Galt's Annals of the Parish", Public Books, 23 January 2017
claims.quote: a very old-fashioned narrator, and therefore reliable
claims.page: essay body, paragraph on Mr. Balwhidder

claims.claim: Le Guin says that in these annals violence is witnessed without participation.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, "B-Sides: John Galt's Annals of the Parish", Public Books, 23 January 2017
claims.page: essay body, paragraph on the riot at the kirk

claims.claim: Le Guin says the annalist leaves it up to the reader to hear what is being told, to imagine it and to feel it.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, "B-Sides: John Galt's Annals of the Parish", Public Books, 23 January 2017
claims.quote: It’s left up to us to hear what’s being told
claims.page: essay body, paragraph on the riot at the kirk

claims.claim: Le Guin says all the material the reader needs to hear, imagine and feel the scene is in those few words, in their choice and in their cadence.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, "B-Sides: John Galt's Annals of the Parish", Public Books, 23 January 2017
claims.quote: in those few words, in their choice and in their cadence
claims.page: essay body, paragraph on the riot at the kirk

claims.claim: Le Guin says Galt's prose works like poetry because every word tells.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, "B-Sides: John Galt's Annals of the Parish", Public Books, 23 January 2017
claims.quote: Galt’s prose works like poetry: every word tells
claims.page: essay body, paragraph on the riot at the kirk

claims.claim: Le Guin says intimate knowledge of one small community may yield psychological and anthropological insights of universal value.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, "B-Sides: John Galt's Annals of the Parish", Public Books, 23 January 2017
claims.quote: may yield psychological and anthropological insights of universal value
claims.page: essay body, paragraph on small-town novels
